name: Omar Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Omar. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on what the company calls the grid modernisation crew. We go round the city and suburbs fitting smart kit onto the old lines: reclosers, which are switches that trip and reset themselves when a branch touches the line, plus sensors and remote-controlled switches. A normal day is up in the bucket fitting a recloser, then on the laptop with control making sure it talks to their system.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's half spanner, half software. I use AI every day, I had it help me write a little script that pulls the sensor readings into a chart so I can spot a line that's running hot. What wears me out is the gap between how fast the kit is and how slow the paperwork is. I can fit a sensor in an hour and wait three weeks for the sign-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are good, people just expected magic. I'd keep showing the crew the little tricks, like the sensor chart. Online I'd post something like, AI didn't change the world but it did fix my spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit let down, because I was looking forward to the job getting more interesting. But money-wise, nothing changes. Amina's a pharmacist, we've got savings and a flat my brother and I bought to rent out. We'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do, keep learning. I'd probably do the online course on grid data I've been eyeing anyway, because the kit we fit is only getting smarter. Keep the savings ticking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the sensor chart actually show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Temperature and load on each section. Last winter one line on Kingsway was running hotter every evening. I flagged it, we went out, there was a cracked connector about to fail. That's the kind of thing I love. A cheap fix before a big outage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew doesn't use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Mick. He says the computer can't smell a burnt joint. He's right, it can't. But it can tell you where to go and sniff. We get on fine.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are good and people just expected magic, and I'd joke online that AI didn't change the world but did fix my spreadsheets.
S0.think: I'd be a bit let down because I wanted the job to get more interesting. Money-wise nothing changes, with my partner's pharmacy job, our savings and the flat my brother and I rent out.
S0.do: Carries on and keeps learning, signing up for an online course in grid data he'd been considering anyway. Keeps adding to savings.
S0.quote: Last winter one line on Kingsway was running hotter every evening. I flagged it, we went out, there was a cracked connector about to fail.
S0.fieldNote: Omar already treats AI as a normal part of the job and built his own sensor tool with it. His only disappointment in this picture is that work wouldn't get more interesting. He's financially very secure, with a rental flat shared with his brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where people like me get busy. Somebody has to fit all the smart kit and keep it running. I'd tell the younger lineworkers to learn the data side now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is good for me. My crew is basically the one doing the change. The bit I'd worry about is the ordinary maintenance crews if the grid starts fixing itself more, fewer call-outs means fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put myself forward for any robot trials the company runs, in the first few months. I'd keep building little tools for the crew. On weekends I might start doing smart-home and solar battery installs on the side, because there'd be demand and I've got the skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, mostly. A little worried for friends on other crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dimitri, mostly, he's on storm repair at the north depot. If the grid gets smart enough to reroute power around faults, they need fewer people waiting on standby. He's not into computers. I'd try and get him onto our crew, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The weekend installs. How serious is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly serious. I've done three for neighbours already, for cash and a curry. If AI is shaking things up, I'd rather have two things going than one. I like having options.

S1.say: I'd say this is when people like me get busy, because someone has to fit and run all the smart kit, and I'd urge younger lineworkers to learn the data side now.
S1.think: This is good for me since my crew is the one carrying out the change. I'd worry about maintenance crews, because a self-repairing grid means fewer call-outs and fewer people.
S1.do: Volunteers for company robot trials in the first few months and keeps building small AI tools for his crew. Starts doing weekend smart-home and solar battery installations on the side.
S1.feel: Calm and mostly excited, with some worry for friends on other crews.
S1.quote: I've done three for neighbours already, for cash and a curry. If AI is shaking things up, I'd rather have two things going than one.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady change as a boost for himself and moves first. His worry is for a friend on a storm crew, whom he'd try to bring over. He's already testing a side business informally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, it's fast, and moaning won't help. Figure out where you fit. I'd say it to the crew straight, and I'd probably post a long thread about what lineworkers should do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be one of the last on the crew to go, because I'd be the one fitting the robots. But two years is two years. After that, I don't know what my job is. Amina's job too, a pharmacy is exactly what AI eats. So I'd be thinking about money more than about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Month one, I'd move a good chunk of our savings into the broad market and into the companies building the robots, because if labour's worth less, owning things is worth more. I'd ask to lead the robot rollout at work, or apply to the robot maker's field team directly. I'd keep the flat and keep the rent coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared exactly. More like the feeling before a big job when you're not sure the drawings are right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move savings into the market in a crisis. What if it goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it goes wrong. I'd keep six months in cash, that's the rule, Amina would insist. The rest I'd put where the money's going. If I'm wrong, we've still got the flat and the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Yusuf and Layla?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf's twelve, he'd think it's cool. I'd tell him, yeah, it is cool, and it's also scary, and both are true. Layla's nine. I'd tell her Dad's figuring it out, which would be true, more or less.

S2.say: I'd say it's real and fast and moaning won't help, so everyone should figure out where they fit, and I'd probably post a long thread about what lineworkers should do.
S2.think: I'd likely be one of the last on my crew to go because I'd be fitting the robots, but after two years I don't know what my job is. With my partner's pharmacy job exposed too, I'd think about money more than work.
S2.do: Moves a large share of savings into broad market funds and robotics companies in the first month while keeping six months in cash. Asks to lead the company's robot rollout or applies to the robot maker's field team, and keeps the rental flat let.
S2.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, like starting a big job unsure the drawings are right.
S2.quote: If labour's worth less, owning things is worth more.
S2.fieldNote: His response to fast AGI is to become an owner rather than just a worker, which fits his comfort with risk. He keeps a firm cash rule set by his partner. He's honest with his son that it's both exciting and scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good warning, use it. Learn the robots, save money, and don't wait for the company to tell you. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is my sweet spot. Enough time to make a move, not so long that I get comfortable. I'd want to be on the robot maker's side of the table by year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do whatever certification the robot makers offer and apply to their field teams. I'd slowly shift some savings into investments, a bit each month. I'd keep the weekend installs going, and maybe go in with my brother on a second rental.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, in a good way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the robot maker's side and not your own company's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the utility will be a customer. Customers get told what to buy. I'd rather be with the people who know how the thing works inside, at least for a few years, then see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about owning things. Is there a risk you put too much in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, there's always that. My brother's more careful than me, which helps. We argue about it at Eid every year. He'd make me keep the cash buffer.

S3.say: I'd say five years is good warning that people should use, by learning the robots and saving rather than waiting for the company to tell them.
S3.think: Five years is my sweet spot, enough time to move but not long enough to get comfortable. I'd want to be on the robot maker's side of the table by year two.
S3.do: Takes robot makers' certifications in the first year and applies to their field teams. Shifts savings into investments monthly, keeps the weekend installation work going and considers a second rental flat with his brother.
S3.feel: Calm and restless in a good way.
S3.quote: Because the utility will be a customer. Customers get told what to buy.
S3.fieldNote: Omar thinks about where power sits in the supply chain, not just about skills. He plans to change employer early rather than wait. His brother acts as a brake on his risk-taking, and he knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads. If you're a lineworker and you can't get ready in ten years, you're choosing not to. I'd probably say it a bit more kindly than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years could be the best thing that happens to my career. I'd be fifty-three, likely running robot crews or doing something with grid data, and the flats and investments would be well along. If work disappears at the end, we'd be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the grid data diploma part-time over the next two years. Keep building the installs into a proper little business. Invest a bit every month. Help other crews learn the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually quite hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd say it more kindly. What's the kind version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kind version is, Mick, mate, you've got ten years, let's sit down one lunch a month and I'll show you one thing. He'd moan, but he'd come. People aren't against learning, they're against feeling stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that worries you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What my kids do for a living. By 2036 Yusuf's twenty-two. If AI does almost any job, what's he for, in work terms? I'd want him to find meaning outside a payslip. I don't have an answer for that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, and lineworkers who don't get ready in that time are choosing not to, though I'd put it more kindly.
S4.think: Ten years could be the best thing for my career, with me running robot crews or doing grid data by fifty-three. If work disappears at the end, the flats and investments would carry us.
S4.do: Takes a part-time grid data diploma over two years and grows the weekend installations into a small business. Invests monthly and helps other crews learn the new tools.
S4.quote: People aren't against learning, they're against feeling stupid.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years feels like an opportunity to him, and his tone toward slower colleagues softens when pushed. His one real worry is what work will mean for his son. He admits he has no answer there.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's too fast for the people around me, even if I'd scrape through. What would help is the robot makers having to train the people they replace, properly, before they're let go, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who looks after the robots in year one. They break, they get confused, they need someone who knows the old grid. For a while, the best robot tech is going to be an old lineworker.

headlineQuote: For a while, the best robot tech is going to be an old lineworker.
portrait: Omar Farah is a 43-year-old lineworker on a grid modernisation crew fitting smart reclosers, sensors and remote switches, and he uses AI daily, including a script he built to chart sensor data. He's married to Amina, a pharmacist, has two children, solid savings and a rental flat shared with his brother. He sees steady change as good for him and already does side installs. Fast AGI only leaves him uneasy because he'd turn to investing and fitting robots, while five and ten years look like chances to move to the robot makers and build a small business, with his main worry being his son's future.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would be too fast for the people around him even if he got through.
whatWouldHelp: Robot makers being required to train the workers they replace properly, before those workers are let go.
